name: Contour Smoothness (Edge Artifact) Analysis
description: Evaluates the mathematical smoothness and geometric continuity of high-contrast edges and object contours. Authentic optical lenses naturally induce slight, continuous blurring (diffraction and optical roll-off) along physical edges. Generative AI models, specifically diffusion-based architectures, frequently struggle with semantic boundary rendering. They often generate object contours that are either mathematically 'too perfect' and unnaturally sharp, or conversely, exhibit severe localized jaggedness, 'melting' artifacts, and erratic gradient steps along what should be a smooth, continuous physical curve.
algorithm: Sub-pixel Canny/Sobel Edge Tracking & Gradient Variance
mechanism: The algorithm isolates object boundaries using sub-pixel precision edge tracing. It then mathematically tracks the gradient magnitude and directional flow along the entire length of these extracted contours. The algorithm flags two specific AI-indicative anomalies: 1) 'Hyper-sharpness'—where a focal edge boundary transitions from object to background instantaneously across a single pixel without any natural optical resolving limits; and 2) 'Micro-jitter' (or Melting)—where a continuously curved edge inexplicably shatters into disjointed, staggered pixel blocks or illogical blurry smudges, ruthlessly exposing the latent decoder's absolute failure to resolve complex, overlapping geometric boundaries.
parameters: Edge Model: Canny/Sobel Sub-pixel, Features: Gradient magnitude variance, Micro-jitter frequency, Optical roll-off curve consistency
accuracy: High (80-92%) - One of the most robust, heavily relied upon, and extensively documented forensic markers for violently unmasking diffusion model generation artifacts.
source: Canny (1986) / Wang (2020) - CNN/Diffusion-generated Images vs. Authentic Optical Geometric Constraints
useCase: Deploying an 'algorithmic magnifying glass' to aggressively expose the microscopic 'melting' or impossible 'hyper-sharp' edge boundaries that immediately out an image as an algorithmic render rather than a physical glass-lens capture.

references.title: Canny, J. (1986). A Computational Approach to Edge Detection. IEEE TPAMI.
Wang, S.Y. et al. (2020). CNN-generated images are surprisingly easy to spot... for now. CVPR.

strengths:
• Phenomenally high hit rate and reliability against both classical CNN-based deepfakes (GANs) and modern high-fidelity Latent Diffusion creations (Stable Diffusion, Midjourney).
• Highly resilient to active camouflage; even when the image is heavily JPEG compressed or intentionally downscaled, the fundamental flawed geometry of 'melting' AI artifacts remains stubbornly detectable.
• Directly exploits the systemic structural weaknesses in AI decoders, which inherently prioritize macro-texture pattern matching over strict geometric edge continuity.
limitations:
• Exceptionally computationally expensive; executing sub-pixel edge tracking and gradient vector calculus across a 4K high-resolution image demands significant CPU resources and tangible processing time.
• Can be falsely triggered by legitimate, highly stylized digital art, vector graphics (SVG exports), or traditional CGI renders, which inherently share the identical 'hyper-sharp', non-optical edge characteristics as AI generations.
• Severe authentic optical motion blur or heavy, creamy out-of-focus background regions (bokeh) can sometimes blind the edge tracker, causing the algorithm to abort tracking in those localized areas.
